name: Antipater (father of Herod the Great)
title: Idumaean strategos and founder of the Herodian dynasty
summary: Antipater was an Idumean politician, diplomat, and founder of a dynasty – the father of Herod the Great. As the son of Antipas, the governor of Idumea, he inherited a political tradition of strategic positioning between great powers. He served as advisor to the Hasmonean king Hyrcanus II and built crucial alliances with Rome. In 47 BC, he supported Julius Caesar militarily during the campaign in Egypt and was appointed prokurator (epitropos) over Judea as a reward. By placing his sons in strategic positions of power, he laid the foundation for the Herodian dynasty. Although Antipater is not mentioned directly in the Bible, his political maneuvers were decisive for the historical context surrounding the gospel accounts, including Jesus' birth during the reign of Herod the Great.

keyEvents.title: Advisor to Hyrcanus II
keyEvents.description: Antipater became a central advisor to the Hasmonean king Hyrcanus II and used his position to strengthen his own family's influence in Judea. He supported Hyrcanus in the rivalry with his brother Aristobulus II and helped secure Roman support for Hyrcanus' claim to the throne.

keyEvents.title: Allied with the Romans
keyEvents.description: Antipater formed an alliance with Julius Caesar and supported him militarily during the campaign in Egypt in 47 BC with a force of around 3,000 soldiers. As a reward, he was appointed procurator over Judea and granted Roman citizenship, giving him a formally recognized position of power.

keyEvents.title: Appointed his sons to positions of power
keyEvents.description: Antipater used his influence to appoint his sons Phasael and Herod as strategoi over Jerusalem and Galilee respectively, thereby laying the dynastic foundation for Herodian rule over Judea.

keyEvents.title: Poisoned by Malichus
keyEvents.description: Antipater was poisoned in 43 BC by his rival Malichus at court. His son Herod avenged the murder shortly afterward by arranging Malichus' death, marking the beginning of Herod's own path to kingship.

keyEvents.title: Historical context for Jesus' birth
keyEvents.description: Antipater's political legacy laid the groundwork for Herod the Great's rule over Judea, during which Jesus was born in Bethlehem according to the Gospel of Matthew.

versions.title: The Idumaean Strategos
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Idumean Strategos' is somewhat unclear. 'Idumean's' could be misunderstood to mean he was a strategos for another Idumean. A more precise title would be 'Idumean Strategos and Founder of the Herodian Dynasty' or similar.; [major] The roles are incomplete. Antipater was primarily a politician and diplomat, not merely a leader and military commander. He should also have the roles 'politician', 'diplomat', and/or 'procurator' (he was appointed procurator over Judea by Caesar).; [minor] The list of children appears correct with Phasael, Herod, Joseph, Pheroras, and Salome. The ID formatting seems reasonable, but it should be verified that these IDs correspond with the rest of the system.; [minor] The summary is good, but could mention that he was appointed procurator (epitropos) over Judea by Julius Caesar in 47 BC, which was a formal office and not merely informal influence.; [minor] The birth year of approximately 113 BC is a reasonable estimate based on Josephus' accounts, though some historians place it closer to 100 BC. It may be worth marking the uncertainty more clearly.; [minor] The reference to Matt 2:1 in the final event is reasonable as a contextual link, but it should be clarified that this concerns Antipater's legacy rather than his direct actions. Otherwise, it is correct that most events lack Bible verses, since Antipater is not a biblical figure.

versions.reason: [minor] The birth year of approx. 113 BC is uncertain. Most historians list the birth year as unknown or simply approx. 110–100 BC. Josephus does not give a precise birth year. It may be safer to write 'unknown – 43 BC' or 'approx. 100–43 BC'.; [minor] The role 'army commander' is somewhat imprecise. Antipater led troops to Egypt for Caesar, but his primary role was political and diplomatic rather than military. The role can be kept, but 'military leader' could be considered or removed in favor of more fitting roles such as 'founder of a dynasty'.; [minor] The ID 'josef-antipaters-sonn' refers to Antipater's son Joseph. Some sources also mention a daughter named Salome (covered by 'salome-antipaters-datter'). The list appears complete based on Josephus, but it is worth noting that the sources vary somewhat regarding the number of children.; [minor] The sixth footnote says 'Antipater's poisoning of Malichus' – this is incorrectly phrased. It was Malichus who poisoned Antipater, not the other way around. The wording should be changed to 'The poisoning of Antipater carried out by Malichus'.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but could be strengthened by mentioning that Antipater was the son of Antipas, who himself was governor of Idumea, to provide further context about the family's political tradition.

footnotes.text: Antipater was of Idumaean origin. The Idumeans (Edomites) were descendants of Esau and were forcibly converted to Judaism under John Hyrcanus I (around 125 BC). This led many Jews of the time to regard the Herodian dynasty as half-Jewish, which affected their legitimacy as rulers over a Jewish people.

The Jewish historian Josephus (Flavius Josephus) is the main source of our knowledge about Antipater. In 'Jewish Antiquities' (Antiquitates Judaicae) book 14 and 'The Jewish War' (Bellum Judaicum) book 1, he provides detailed accounts of Antipater's political career and alliance with Rome.

The name Antipater (Greek: Ἀντίπατρος) means 'in place of the father' or 'like the father'. It was a common Greek name that reflected Hellenistic cultural influence even among Idumaean families during this period.

Antipater's alliance with Julius Caesar in 47 BC during the siege of Alexandria was a political turning point. According to Josephus, he is said to have brought about 3,000 Jewish soldiers to the rescue and convinced the Nabateans and Syrians to support Caesar. As a reward, he received Roman citizenship and the title epitropos (procurator) over Judea.

Archaeological finds from Idumea, including ostraka (inscribed pottery shards) from Maresha and other cities, confirm the cultural and religious diversity in the region during Antipater's time, with a mix of Edomite, Arab, and Hellenistic influence.

The poisoning of Antipater, carried out by his rival Malichus in 43 BC, illustrates the intense power struggle in Judea during the late Hasmonean period. Josephus recounts that Herodes avenged his father's death by arranging the murder of Malichus shortly afterward, marking the beginning of Herodes' own path to royal power.

Antipater's wife Kypros was of Nabatean origin, highlighting the family's strategic marriage alliances with neighboring powers. The Nabateans controlled important trade routes in the region, and the alliance further strengthened Antipater's position.

In rabbinic tradition, the Herodian dynasty was often viewed with suspicion precisely because of its Idumean origins. The Talmud (Bava Batra 3b–4a) refers to Herodes as a 'slave from the Hasmonean house,' a designation reflecting the enduring doubt about the family's Jewish legitimacy—an legacy that began with Antipater.
